text:
I need help with an open letter from our tenants' association to our property management company. We plan to post it in the lobby and send it to the local TV station. I'm the association's secretary.

Facts:
- Our building has 9 stories, 112 apartments and one elevator.
- The elevator was out of service on 41 days this year, including one stretch of 12 days in August.
- 23 of our residents are over 75, and 6 use wheelchairs or walkers.
- The management company says a new controller part is on order and should arrive in 6 to 8 weeks. They said the same thing in June.
- The city inspected the elevator in September and gave it a passing certificate.
- 74 households signed our petition asking for a second elevator. Management says that would cost about $400,000 and can't be done in this building.

About 400 words.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter asks for and how it reads:

1. **What exactly do you want management to do, and by when?** Your petition asks for a second elevator, but management has already said no on cost and feasibility, and a TV audience may take their side on that. Would the association also accept, or prefer, things they can't easily refuse? For example, a firm delivery date for the part with written proof of the order, a service contract with guaranteed repair times, help for residents who can't use the stairs during outages, or an independent study of whether a second elevator is feasible. And do you want a deadline for their reply?
2. **What happened to residents during the outages, especially the 12 days in August?** For example, people who were stuck in their apartments, missed medical appointments, or were carried down the stairs. Did any of them agree to have their story or name used? One real example will do more than all the numbers.
3. **What has management said or done since June?** Did they answer the petition in writing, offer anything for the interim, or explain why the June part never came? And do you know if the controller part caused most of the 41 days?
4. **Names and sign-off:** the building, its address or neighborhood, the management company, and the association. Should the letter be signed by you as secretary, by the board, or "on behalf of the 74 households"? Is there a contact for the TV station?
5. **How sharp should it be?** Firm but civil, so the door stays open, or openly confrontational because talks have failed? Also, should the letter mention the passed September inspection up front? Management will likely use it to say the elevator is fine.

If you don't know some of these, tell me and I'll write the letter without them rather than guess.

1. We want three things: a written date for the repair, a stair-climbing chair with trained staff for residents who can't walk the stairs, and a rent credit for outage days. On the second elevator, we have no engineer's opinion, so management may be right that it can't be done. I don't have a deadline in mind for their reply. In return, we can meet them any weekday evening. We can also keep a list of residents who need help on the stairs and share it with management for emergencies.

2. During the 12 days in August, a resident on the 8th floor missed two dialysis appointments. I don't know yet if they'd agree to be named.

3. I don't know about anything in writing beyond the "6 to 8 weeks" answer. I also don't know if the controller part caused most of the 41 days.

4. The building is Harbor View Apartments, 220 Grant Street. The company is Keystone Property Group, and the regional manager is Diane Weller. I'm Rosa Delgado, secretary. We can't speak for all 112 households, only the 74 that signed, so I'd say sign it on their behalf. A reporter at Channel 7 said she'd come when we post it on the 1st of next month.

5. Firm but civil. Yes, mention the inspection. It only checks that the elevator is safe. It doesn't look at how often it breaks down.

I've drafted the letter at about 400 words, dated for the day you post it.

<final_document>
December 1, 2026

**An open letter to Keystone Property Group**
Attention: Diane Weller, Regional Manager

From the Harbor View Apartments Tenants' Association, 220 Grant Street

Dear Ms. Weller,

Harbor View has 9 floors, 112 apartments and one elevator. This year that elevator has been out of service on 41 days. The longest outage lasted 12 days in August.

For many of our neighbors, a broken elevator means they can't leave home. Twenty-three residents are over 75, and six use wheelchairs or walkers. During the August outage, a resident on the 8th floor missed two dialysis appointments.

In June, Keystone told us a new controller part was on order and would arrive in 6 to 8 weeks. We are still hearing that same answer. We have received nothing in writing beyond that estimate.

We know the city inspected the elevator in September and gave it a passing certificate, and we are glad it is safe. But that inspection only checks safety. It doesn't look at how often the elevator breaks down. A safe elevator that isn't running does nothing for a neighbor who needs to get to dialysis.

74 households signed our petition asking for a second elevator. You have told us it would cost about $400,000 and can't be done in this building. We have no engineer's opinion that says otherwise. So today we are asking for three things that can be done:

1. **A written date for the repair.** We also ask for confirmation that the part has actually been ordered.
2. **A stair-climbing chair at Harbor View, with trained staff.** Residents who can't use the stairs need a way to get in and out of the building when the elevator is down.
3. **A rent credit for every day the elevator is out of service.**

We will do our part too. The association will keep a list of residents who need help on the stairs. We will share it with Keystone so your staff know who to check on during an outage or an emergency. We can meet with you on any weekday evening that works for you.

Please reply in writing. We will post your reply in the lobby next to this letter so every resident can read it.

Sincerely,

Rosa Delgado
Secretary, Harbor View Apartments Tenants' Association
On behalf of the 74 households who signed our petition
</final_document>

A few things to check before you post it:

- **The dialysis resident:** The letter doesn't name them or their apartment, but a resident on the 8th floor who needs dialysis may be easy for neighbors to identify. Ask them before it goes up, even if they stay unnamed. If they agree to be named, or to talk to Channel 7, that will be the strongest part of the story.
- **The 74 signatures:** Those households signed a petition for a second elevator, not for these three requests. Consider checking quickly that they're comfortable having their names behind these requests. If Keystone or the reporter asks, you'll have an answer.
- **The last line:** I added the promise to post Keystone's reply in the lobby. It shows good faith and gives them a reason to answer properly. Cut it if the association doesn't want to commit to that.
- **What I left out:** The letter doesn't say the controller part caused the outages, and it doesn't set a reply deadline, since you didn't know or didn't want those. If you later learn what caused most of the 41 days, it's worth adding.
